meta.title: Who really said "Many people think they are thinking when they are merely rearranging their prejudices"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Knute Rockne — he quoted it in 1926 and said so. Earliest known source: Bishop William F. Oldham, Zion's Herald, 7 November 1906.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Many people think they are thinking when they are merely rearranging their prejudices'?
meta.ogDescription: Rockne printed it in quotation marks and disclaimed it. The trail leads back to Bishop William F. Oldham in Zion's Herald, 1906.

answer.label: Not Knute Rockne — he quoted it and said so
answer.sourceLine: The earliest known appearance is a report in the Boston Methodist weekly Zion’s Herald on 7 November 1906, which credited Bishop William Fitzjames Oldham with the “bon mot” that some people “think they are thinking when they are merely rearranging their prejudices.” Knute Rockne did print a version in a 1926 newspaper column — but he put it in quotation marks and said he had heard it somewhere, explicitly disclaiming authorship.
answer.confidenceText: Quote Investigator calls Oldham the leading candidate but labels the conclusion tentative — treat the origin as earliest-known, not settled.

source.heading: Where the line actually first appears

docMeta.dd: Vol. 84, no. 45 — 7 November 1906, p. 1433, col. 2 (Boston, Mass.)
Bishop William Fitzjames Oldham, reported second-hand in a “Notes” column
The Des Moines Register, 5 November 1926, p. 11 — in quotation marks, with a disclaimer

source.excerpt: Bishop Oldham scored with his audience with a bon mot to the effect that some people “think they are thinking when they are merely rearranging their prejudices.”
trail: 1906 — Zion’s Herald (Boston) reports Bishop Oldham’s quip about people who “think they are thinking”; this is the earliest close match Quote Investigator has located ↗.
1926 — Knute Rockne opens a column in The Des Moines Register (5 November, p. 11) with the saying in quotation marks, writing that he had heard the remark once upon a time ↗.
1946 & 1949 — newspapers in Louisiana and Illinois assign the line to William James and then Edward R. Murrow ↗, long after it was in general circulation.
2017 — Quote Investigator concludes that Oldham is the leading candidate for coiner, tentatively ↗, and that the William James attribution is weakly supported.
source.excerptNote: Note the framing: the reporter writes “to the effect that,” so even the 1906 item is a paraphrase of something said aloud. No text written by Oldham himself has been located containing this sentence.
source.rightsNote: The earliest documented text is the 7 November 1906 issue of Zion’s Herald, published in the United States well before 1931, so that reporting is in the public domain. Rockne’s 1926 Des Moines Register column is likewise pre-1931. The saying itself is a short aphorism of uncertain coinage, and no post-1930 copyrighted work is the source of the popular wording.

author.name: William Fitzjames Oldham
author.heading: The bishop with the better line
author.metaLine: 1854–1937 · Methodist Episcopal bishop & missionary to South Asia
author.bio: Born in Bangalore to an Irish family, Oldham converted to Methodism in 1873 and sailed for Singapore in 1885, where he founded the Anglo-Chinese School the following year. He was appointed Missionary Bishop of Southern Asia in 1904 and served as a general bishop of the Methodist Episcopal Church from 1916 until his death. He was a working preacher and lecturer, which is exactly the setting in which the line first surfaces — as a platform quip reported by a religious weekly, not a sentence from a book.

misattribution.heading: Four famous names, none of them the source
misattribution.intro: This saying has been hung on at least four well-known people, in each case decades after it was already circulating. The pattern is always the same: someone repeats a line they heard, and the repetition becomes the attribution.

items.scope: Most common on sports and coaching quote sites
items.why: Rockne’s column in The Des Moines Register of 5 November 1926 opens with the saying inside quotation marks and adds that he had heard the remark once upon a time — an explicit disclaimer of authorship ↗.

The “A great many people think they are thinking…” wording was credited to James in a 1946 Louisiana newspaper, 36 years after his death; Quote Investigator reports the support for the James attribution is “quite weak” ↗.
A Mattoon, Illinois newspaper credited Murrow with a “re-arranging their prejudices” version in 1949 — more than forty years after the saying first appeared in print ↗.
In 1926 the botanist was credited with the cousin line that people who do not think should at least re-arrange their prejudices once in a while — a variant, not the source ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented appearance is Zion’s Herald, 7 November 1906, crediting Bishop William Fitzjames Oldham — whom Quote Investigator calls the leading candidate, while noting the conclusion is tentative ↗.

context.heading: A quip that outran everyone who said it
lead: This is a textbook “orphan aphorism.” It starts life as a line delivered from a platform, gets reported second-hand in a church weekly, and then circulates for decades with no owner — so each generation staples it to whoever sounds most plausible. A football coach in 1926, a psychologist in 1946, a broadcaster in 1949.

What makes the Rockne version unusual is how clearly he disowned it. His 1926 column opens with the saying in quotation marks and the admission that he had heard it before; the quotation marks were doing exactly the job quotation marks are supposed to do. Ninety years of reprinting erased them.
detailsBody: The 1946 attribution to William James is the version most people meet today, usually in the form “A great many people think they are thinking…” It surfaced 36 years after James died, and Quote Investigator reports finding no closely matching statement in his work — describing the support for the James attribution as “quite weak.”

A cousin saying circulated under Luther Burbank’s name in 1926: that people who do not think should at least re-arrange their prejudices once in a while. It is a variant of the same joke, not evidence of a separate origin.
context.pull: Rockne put it in quotation marks. History took the quotation marks off.
